lessons.title: Induced potential, transformers and the National Grid
lessons.summary: Learn how moving a conductor through a magnetic field induces a potential difference, how this generator effect is used in alternators, dynamos and microphones, and how transformers change voltage so electricity can be sent efficiently across the National Grid.
objectives: I can describe the generator effect and the factors that affect the size and direction of an induced potential difference.
I can explain how an alternator produces a.c. and a dynamo produces d.c., and sketch their output traces.
I can explain how a moving-coil microphone works.
I can use the transformer equations Vp / Vs = np / ns and Vp Ip = Vs Is.
I can explain why the National Grid uses step-up and step-down transformers.

activities.title: The generator effect
activities.content:
## Making electricity from movement

The motor effect turns electricity into movement. The reverse also works: **if a conductor moves through a magnetic field, or a magnetic field changes around a conductor, a potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor.** This is the **generator effect** (electromagnetic induction).

If the conductor is part of a **complete circuit**, the induced p.d. drives an **induced current**. Push a magnet into a coil connected to a sensitive ammeter and the needle flicks; pull it out and the needle flicks the other way; hold it still and nothing happens.

### Rules for the induced p.d.
You get a **bigger** induced p.d. by:
- moving the conductor or magnet **faster**,
- using a **stronger magnet** (greater flux density),
- using a coil with **more turns**,
- using a coil with a **larger area**.

You **reverse** the direction of the induced p.d. by:
- reversing the direction of **movement**,
- reversing the **magnetic field** (swapping the poles).

### The induced current opposes the change
An induced current has its **own** magnetic field. This field always acts **against the change that produced it**. Push a N pole into a coil and the induced current makes the near end of the coil a N pole too, repelling the magnet. This is why you have to do work to turn a generator: the induced current fights the motion. That work is the source of the electrical energy.

A microphone, a bicycle dynamo, a power station generator and a wind turbine all use the generator effect.

question.text: A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a sensitive ammeter. Which THREE changes would INCREASE the size of the induced current?
question.explanation: Moving the magnet faster, using a stronger magnet and using more turns all increase the induced p.d. and current. Holding the magnet still induces nothing, and pulling it out instead of pushing in only reverses the direction.

options.text: Push the magnet in faster
Use a stronger magnet
Use a coil with more turns
Hold the magnet stationary inside the coil
options.feedback: No movement or change of field means no induced p.d.

options.text: Pull the magnet out instead of pushing it in
options.feedback: This reverses the direction but not the size.

activities.title: Alternators and dynamos
activities.content:
## Generators

A generator is a motor run backwards: a **coil is rotated in a magnetic field** (or a magnet is rotated inside a coil). As each side of the coil cuts through the field lines, a p.d. is induced.

### The alternator: a.c.
As the coil turns, each side moves **up** through the field for half a turn and **down** for the other half, so the induced p.d. **reverses every half turn**. The coil ends are connected to two separate **slip rings** with brushes pressing on them. The output is **alternating current (a.c.)**.

On an oscilloscope the trace is a smooth **sine wave**: p.d. rises to a peak, falls through zero, reaches a negative peak and returns.

```
 a.c.  +|   /\        /\
        |  /  \      /  \
       0|-/----\----/----\---- time
        |       \  /      \  /
       -|        \/        \/
```

- The p.d. is **largest** when the coil sides are cutting field lines fastest (coil horizontal, moving straight across the lines).
- The p.d. is **zero** when the coil is vertical and its sides move parallel to the field, cutting no lines.

### The dynamo: d.c.
Swap the slip rings for a **split-ring commutator** (as in a motor). Every half turn the connections swap just as the p.d. is about to reverse, so the output always has the **same sign**. The trace is a series of humps that never go below zero.

```
 d.c.  +|   /\    /\    /\
        |  /  \  /  \  /  \
       0|-/----\/----\/----\-- time
```

This is **direct current** but not a steady one; it pulses.

### Changing the trace
Spin the coil **faster**: the peaks get **taller** (bigger p.d.) and **closer together** (higher frequency). Use a stronger magnet or more turns: taller peaks only.

question.text: An alternator is turned twice as fast as before. How does the oscilloscope trace change?
question.hint: Faster cutting of field lines means bigger p.d.; faster rotation also means more cycles per second.
question.explanation: Turning the coil faster makes it cut field lines more quickly, increasing the induced p.d. (taller peaks), and completes more cycles each second (peaks closer together, higher frequency).

options.text: The peaks become taller and closer together
The peaks become taller but stay the same distance apart
The peaks become shorter and further apart
The trace stays exactly the same

question.text: Match each feature to the correct type of generator.
question.hint: The commutator is the part that keeps the output the same sign.
question.explanation: An alternator uses slip rings and gives a.c. that changes sign; a dynamo uses a split-ring commutator so the output is always the same sign (d.c.).

activities.title: Microphones
activities.content:
## Sound into electricity

A **moving-coil microphone** is a loudspeaker in reverse.

1. Sound waves reach a thin, flexible **diaphragm** and make it **vibrate**. The vibrations copy the pressure variations of the sound.
2. A small **coil** is attached to the diaphragm and sits in the field of a **permanent magnet**. As the diaphragm vibrates, the coil **moves back and forth through the magnetic field**.
3. By the generator effect, a **p.d. is induced** across the coil. Because the coil's motion reverses with every vibration, the induced p.d. is **alternating**.
4. The induced a.c. has the **same frequency** as the sound wave, and a **louder** sound (bigger diaphragm movement) gives a **larger** p.d.

So the microphone converts the **pressure variations in a sound wave into variations in current** in an electrical circuit. That signal can be amplified, recorded or sent to a loudspeaker, which turns it back into sound using the motor effect.

| | Loudspeaker | Microphone |
|---|---|---|
| Effect used | motor effect | generator effect |
| Input | alternating current | sound wave |
| Output | sound wave | alternating p.d. |

question.text: Put the steps in order to describe how a moving-coil microphone works.
question.hint: Begin with the sound wave arriving.
question.explanation: Sound makes the diaphragm vibrate; the attached coil moves in the magnetic field; a p.d. is induced; the alternating p.d. matches the sound frequency.
order: Sound waves make the diaphragm vibrate
The coil attached to the diaphragm moves back and forth in the magnetic field
A potential difference is induced across the coil by the generator effect
The alternating p.d. has the same frequency as the sound wave

activities.title: Transformers
activities.content:
## Changing the voltage

A **transformer** changes the size of an alternating p.d. It has two coils of insulated wire wound on the same **soft iron core**:
- the **primary coil** is connected to the a.c. input,
- the **secondary coil** gives the output.

### How it works
1. The alternating current in the primary produces a **changing magnetic field**.
2. The iron core channels this field through the secondary coil (iron is easily magnetised, and a laminated core reduces energy losses).
3. The changing field in the secondary **induces an alternating p.d.** across it by the generator effect.

A transformer **only works with a.c.** A steady d.c. current gives a steady field, and a steady field induces nothing.

### The turns equation
$$\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{n_p}{n_s}$$

- $V_p$, $V_s$ = p.d. across the primary and secondary coils (V)
- $n_p$, $n_s$ = number of turns on the primary and secondary

- A **step-up** transformer has **more turns on the secondary** than the primary, so $V_s > V_p$.
- A **step-down** transformer has **fewer turns on the secondary**, so $V_s < V_p$.

### The power equation
If the transformer is **100 % efficient**, power in = power out:

$$V_p I_p = V_s I_s$$

So when a transformer steps the voltage **up**, it steps the current **down** by the same factor, and vice versa.

activities.title: Worked example: transformer calculations
activities.content:
**A phone charger transformer has 2300 turns on its primary and 50 turns on its secondary. The primary is connected to the 230 V mains. Find the output p.d.**

$\dfrac{V_p}{V_s} = \dfrac{n_p}{n_s}$ so $\dfrac{230}{V_s} = \dfrac{2300}{50}$

$V_s = \dfrac{230 \times 50}{2300} = 5$ V

Fewer turns on the secondary: a step-down transformer.

**The charger delivers 2.0 A at 5 V. Assuming 100 % efficiency, find the current drawn from the mains.**

$V_p I_p = V_s I_s$

$230 \times I_p = 5 \times 2.0 = 10$ W

$I_p = \dfrac{10}{230} = 0.043$ A (about 43 mA)

**A step-up transformer has 400 turns on the primary and an input of 25 kV. The output is 400 kV. How many turns are on the secondary?**

$\dfrac{25\,000}{400\,000} = \dfrac{400}{n_s}$

$n_s = \dfrac{400 \times 400\,000}{25\,000} = 6400$ turns

A quick check: the voltage goes up 16 times, so the turns must go up 16 times too: 400 × 16 = 6400.

question.text: A transformer has 800 turns on its primary coil and 40 turns on its secondary coil. The input p.d. is 240 V. Calculate the output p.d.
question.hint: Vp / Vs = np / ns, so Vs = Vp × ns ÷ np.

question.text: A transformer steps 230 V down to 11.5 V to power a lamp that draws a current of 4.0 A. Assuming the transformer is 100 % efficient, calculate the current in the primary coil.
question.hint: Vp Ip = Vs Is. Find the output power first, then divide by the primary voltage.

activities.title: The National Grid
activities.content:
## Getting electricity across the country

The **National Grid** is the system of **cables and transformers** that links power stations to homes, schools and factories.

Power stations generate electricity at about **25 kV**. Sending it across the country at this voltage would waste an enormous amount of energy heating the cables, because a large current in a resistor transfers a lot of power to thermal stores ($P = I^2 R$).

### The solution: transmit at high voltage, low current
1. **Step-up transformers** at the power station raise the p.d. to **400 000 V (400 kV)** or so. Because $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$, raising the voltage 16 times lowers the current 16 times.
2. The cables then carry a **small current**, so the heating losses in the cables are much **smaller** (a 16-times smaller current means 256-times less heating in the same cable). The transmission is far more **efficient**.
3. **Step-down transformers** near towns reduce the p.d. in stages to **230 V**, which is **safe** for use in homes.

### Why not just use thicker cables?
Thicker cables have lower resistance, but they are heavier, need bigger pylons and cost much more. Raising the voltage is cheaper and more effective.

### Why a.c.?
Transformers only work with alternating current, and the whole system depends on transformers. That is why mains electricity in the UK is **a.c. at 50 Hz**.

question.text:
A power station generates electricity at 25 kV with a current of 8000 A. A step-up transformer raises the p.d. to 400 kV for transmission.

(a) The primary coil of the transformer has 500 turns. Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil. (2 marks)

(b) Assuming the transformer is 100 % efficient, calculate the current in the transmission cables. (2 marks)

(c) Explain why transmitting at 400 kV rather than 25 kV makes the National Grid more efficient. (2 marks)
question.hint: For (b), power stays the same: 25 000 × 8000 = 400 000 × Is.
question.explanation: (a) 25 000 / 400 000 = 500 / ns, so ns = 500 × 16 = 8000 turns. (b) Vp Ip = Vs Is: 25 000 × 8000 = 400 000 × Is, so Is = 500 A. (c) A higher p.d. means a smaller current for the same power. Less current means less energy is transferred to the thermal store of the cables (less heating), so less power is wasted.

markScheme.criterion: Uses Vp Ip = Vs Is / power = 200 MW
Higher p.d. means a smaller current in the cables
So less energy is wasted heating the cables / less power lost

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Generator effect**: moving a conductor through a field (or changing the field around it) **induces a p.d.**, and a current if there is a complete circuit. Bigger with faster movement, stronger magnet, more turns. The induced current's field **opposes the change** that caused it.
- **Alternator** (slip rings) gives **a.c.**: a sine-wave trace. **Dynamo** (split-ring commutator) gives pulsing **d.c.**. Spinning faster gives taller, closer peaks.
- **Microphone**: sound vibrates a diaphragm and coil in a magnetic field, inducing an a.c. of the same frequency.
- **Transformers** work only with a.c.: $\dfrac{V_p}{V_s} = \dfrac{n_p}{n_s}$ and, if 100 % efficient, $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$. Step-up: more secondary turns; step-down: fewer.
- **National Grid**: step up to ~400 kV to make the current small and cut heating losses in cables, then step down to 230 V for safe use.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: a potential difference is induced in a coil when a magnet is held perfectly still inside it.
practiceQuestions.hint: The field must be changing or the conductor must be moving.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Induction needs relative movement or a changing magnetic field. A stationary magnet induces nothing.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Which of these is an example of the generator effect?
practiceQuestions.hint: Generator effect: movement in, electricity out.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A bicycle dynamo turns the motion of the wheel into an induced p.d. A loudspeaker and a motor use the motor effect; an electromagnet is just a current producing a field.

options.text: A bicycle dynamo lighting a lamp
A loudspeaker producing sound
An electromagnet lifting scrap metal
A d.c. motor turning a fan

metadata.blanksText: An alternator uses ___ rings and produces alternating current, whereas a dynamo uses a split-ring ___ and produces direct current.

practiceQuestions.hint: The dynamo part has the same name as the part in a motor.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Alternator: slip rings, a.c. Dynamo: split-ring commutator, d.c.

practiceQuestions.text: At which position of a rotating coil in an alternator is the induced p.d. zero?
practiceQuestions.hint: The p.d. is zero when the sides of the coil are not cutting any field lines.
practiceQuestions.explanation: When the coil is vertical, its sides move parallel to the field lines and cut none, so the induced p.d. is zero. The p.d. is maximum when the coil is horizontal.

options.text: When the coil is vertical and its sides move parallel to the field
When the coil is horizontal and its sides cut straight across the field
options.feedback: That is where the p.d. is greatest.

options.text: At every position; it is never zero
Only when the coil stops moving

practiceQuestions.text: A transformer has 100 turns on the primary and 2000 turns on the secondary. The input is 12 V. Calculate the output p.d.
practiceQuestions.hint: The turns increase 20 times, so the voltage does too.

practiceQuestions.text: A step-down transformer converts 230 V to 9.2 V. There are 1500 turns on the primary coil. Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil.

A transformer supplies 20 V at 3.0 A to a toy train. The primary is connected to 230 V. Assuming 100 % efficiency, calculate the current in the primary coil. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
practiceQuestions.hint: Vp Ip = Vs Is. Output power = 20 × 3.0 = 60 W.

practiceQuestions.text: A step-up transformer at a power station raises 25 kV to 275 kV. The current in the primary is 4400 A. Assuming 100 % efficiency, calculate the current in the secondary in amps.
Explain why a transformer does not work with a direct current supply.
practiceQuestions.hint: What does the secondary coil need in order to have a p.d. induced in it?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A steady d.c. produces a constant magnetic field in the core. A p.d. is only induced in the secondary when the magnetic field through it is changing, so with d.c. no p.d. is induced (except briefly when switching on or off).

markScheme.criterion: d.c. produces a constant / unchanging magnetic field
A p.d. is only induced by a changing magnetic field

practiceQuestions.text:
A wind turbine produces electricity that is fed into the National Grid.

(a) Describe how the rotation of the turbine blades produces an alternating potential difference. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why the electricity from the turbine passes through a step-up transformer before it is sent along the grid cables, and why a step-down transformer is used before the electricity reaches houses. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (a), a coil rotating in a magnetic field cuts field lines. For (b), think about heating losses in cables and safety.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) The blades turn a coil in a magnetic field (or a magnet inside a coil). The coil sides cut through field lines, inducing a p.d.; the direction reverses every half turn so the output alternates. (b) Stepping up the voltage lowers the current, reducing energy lost as heat in the cables and making transmission more efficient. Stepping down gives a safer 230 V for homes.

markScheme.criterion: The blades rotate a coil in a magnetic field (or a magnet inside a coil), cutting field lines
A p.d. is induced whose direction reverses every half turn, giving a.c.
Step-up transformer increases voltage and so decreases current, reducing energy lost as heat in the cables
Step-down transformer reduces the voltage to a safe level (230 V) for homes

practiceQuestions.text: A coil of wire connected to a voltmeter is rotated between the poles of a magnet. Which THREE changes would INCREASE the size of the induced potential difference?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about how quickly field lines are cut, how strong the field is and how much wire is cutting it.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Rotating the coil faster cuts the field lines more quickly, a stronger magnet provides more field lines to cut, and more turns mean more wire cutting the field; all three increase the induced p.d. Stopping the coil induces nothing, and reversing the direction of rotation only reverses the direction of the induced p.d.

options.text: Rotate the coil faster
Replace the magnet with a stronger one
Use a coil with more turns of wire
Stop the coil so it is stationary between the poles
options.feedback: With no movement, no field lines are cut, so no p.d. is induced.

options.text: Rotate the coil in the opposite direction at the same speed
options.feedback: This reverses the direction of the induced p.d. but not its size.

practiceQuestions.text: The handle of a hand-cranked alternator is turned at half the speed it was before. How does the trace on the oscilloscope change?
practiceQuestions.hint: Slower turning means field lines are cut more slowly and fewer cycles are completed each second.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Turning the coil more slowly means it cuts field lines less quickly, so the induced p.d. is smaller and the peaks are shorter. It also completes fewer cycles each second, so the frequency halves and the peaks are further apart.

options.text: The peaks become shorter and further apart
The peaks become shorter but stay the same distance apart
options.feedback: The frequency halves as well, so the peaks spread out.

options.text: The peaks become taller and closer together
options.feedback: That is what happens when the coil is turned faster.

options.text: The trace does not change

practiceQuestions.text: Match each description to the type of generator it applies to.
practiceQuestions.hint: Slip rings let the output change sign; a commutator swaps the connections every half turn so it never does.
practiceQuestions.explanation: An alternator uses slip rings, so the output p.d. changes sign every half turn and it produces alternating current. A dynamo uses a split-ring commutator, which swaps the coil's connections to the outside circuit every half turn so the output always has the same sign (direct current).

pairs.left: Output p.d. varies in size but always has the same sign
The coil's connections to the outside circuit are swapped every half turn

practiceQuestions.text: Put these steps in order to describe how a moving-coil microphone converts a spoken word into an electrical signal.
practiceQuestions.hint: Begin with the sound wave hitting the diaphragm and end with the signal leaving the microphone.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The pressure variations in the sound wave push and pull the diaphragm, which vibrates with the attached coil at the frequency of the sound. The moving coil cuts the field lines of the permanent magnet, inducing a p.d. by the generator effect, and this alternating p.d. is the electrical signal, which copies the pattern of the sound.
order: Pressure variations in the sound wave push and pull on the diaphragm
The diaphragm and the coil attached to it vibrate at the frequency of the sound
The moving coil cuts the field lines of the permanent magnet, so a p.d. is induced across it
The induced alternating p.d. is sent out as an electrical signal that matches the pattern of the sound

practiceQuestions.text: A doorbell transformer has 1200 turns on its primary coil and 60 turns on its secondary coil. The primary is connected to the 230 V mains. Calculate the output p.d.
practiceQuestions.hint: $V_p \div V_s = n_p \div n_s$, so $V_s = V_p \times n_s \div n_p$.

practiceQuestions.text: A step-down transformer converts 230 V to 23 V to run a heater that draws a current of 3.0 A. Assuming the transformer is 100 % efficient, calculate the current in the primary coil.
practiceQuestions.hint: $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$. Work out the power delivered to the heater first, then divide by the primary p.d.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Output power $= V_s I_s = 23 \times 3.0 = 69$ W. $I_p = 69 \div 230 = 0.30$ A.

practiceQuestions.text:
A gas-fired power station generates electricity at 33 kV with a current of 4000 A. A step-up transformer raises the p.d. to 132 kV before it enters the National Grid.

(a) The primary coil of the transformer has 600 turns. Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil. (2 marks)

(b) Assuming the transformer is 100 % efficient, calculate the current in the transmission cables. (2 marks)

(c) Explain why transmitting the electricity at 132 kV rather than 33 kV reduces the energy wasted in the cables. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (a), the p.d. is multiplied by 4, so the turns are too. For (b), the power is the same on both sides: 33 000 × 4000 = 132 000 × I.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) $V_p \div V_s = n_p \div n_s$: $33\,000 \div 132\,000 = 600 \div n_s$, so $n_s = 600 \times 4 = 2400$ turns. (b) $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$: $33\,000 \times 4000 = 132\,000 \times I_s$, so $I_s = 1000$ A. (c) For the same power, a higher p.d. means a smaller current in the cables. A smaller current transfers less energy to the thermal store of the cables, so less power is wasted as heat.

markScheme.criterion: Uses Vp Ip = Vs Is / power = 132 MW
Higher p.d. means a smaller current in the cables
So less energy is wasted heating the cables / less power lost
